nodes.name: router
setup: ip tuntap add dev pl-ab mode tun && ip tuntap add dev pl-ba mode tun && ip link set pl-ab up && ip link set pl-ba up && sysctl -qw net.ipv4.conf.pl-ab.rp_filter=0 net.ipv4.conf.pl-ba.rp_filter=0 && ip rule add iif eth0 table 100 && ip route add default dev pl-ab table 100 && ip rule add iif eth1 table 101 && ip route add default dev pl-ba table 101

checks.name: 100 writes of 10 bytes arrive as however many read()s the receiver happens to do — and Nagle changes the segments
run: ${BIN}/socklab serve -addr 198.18.201.10:7001 -mode reads -for 3s > ${EVIDENCE}/reads.txt & S=$!; tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -w ${EVIDENCE}/writes.pcap 'tcp dst port 7001' 2>/dev/null & T=$!; sleep 0.5; ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ${BIN}/socklab writes -to 198.18.201.10:7001 -n 100 -size 10; sleep 0.3; ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ${BIN}/socklab writes -to 198.18.201.10:7001 -n 100 -size 10 -nodelay=false; sleep 0.5; kill -INT $T; wait $S; grep reads: ${EVIDENCE}/reads.txt; echo 'data segments per client connection (count, client address):'; tcpdump -nn -r ${EVIDENCE}/writes.pcap '(ip[2:2] - ((ip[0]&0xf)<<2) - ((tcp[12]&0xf0)>>2)) > 0' 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -c
expect_contains: sent 1000 bytes; the server's read() returned them in

checks.name: shrink this client's ephemeral range to 32 ports (60000–60031) — a namespace setting, the host is untouched

hold connections open to one server port: 32 succeed, the 33rd fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL; at the same moment 32 more to a second port of the same server succeed — ports run out per destination, not per host
the client closed those 64 connections first, so it now holds 64 TIME_WAITs (32 per destination port) — they block those tuples for 60 s
run: for p in 7002 7003; do echo "TIME_WAIT to :$p: $(ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :$p | wc -l)"; done

checks.name: connect and close 300 times where the SERVER closes first: all succeed with 32 ports — the client keeps no TIME_WAIT
run: ${BIN}/socklab churn -to 198.18.201.10:7004 -n 300 -server-closes; echo "client TIME_WAIT to :7004: $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :7004 | wc -l); server TIME_WAIT on :7004: $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-server ss -Htan state time-wait sport = :7004 | wc -l)"

checks.name: the same where the CLIENT closes first: each close leaves a 60 s TIME_WAIT on the client; after 32, EADDRNOTAVAIL
run: ${BIN}/socklab churn -to 198.18.201.10:7005 -n 100; echo "client TIME_WAIT to :7005: $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :7005 | wc -l)"

checks.name: tcp_tw_reuse=1 (default 2 = loopback only) lets connect() reuse a TIME_WAIT port once it is 1 s old: 32 more, then EADDRNOTAVAIL again — reuse buys ports per second, not unlimited ports
run: sysctl -qw net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 && sleep 1.2 && ${BIN}/socklab churn -to 198.18.201.10:7005 -n 100; sysctl -qw net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=2 net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range='32768 60999'; sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range

checks.name: add 5 ms each way (10 ms RTT) so connection setup costs something
1000 requests, 20 workers, no keep-alive: 1000 connections, each request pays the handshake (p50 ≈ 2 RTT); the server closes first and keeps the TIME_WAITs
run: tw0=$(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :8080 | wc -l); sw0=$(ip netns exec nl-sockets-server ss -Htan state time-wait sport = :8080 | wc -l); ${BIN}/socklab http -url 'http://198.18.201.10:8080/obj?size=10000' -n 1000 -c 20 -keepalive=false; echo "  new TIME_WAIT — client: $(( $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :8080 | wc -l) - tw0 )), server: $(( $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-server ss -Htan state time-wait sport = :8080 | wc -l) - sw0 ))"

checks.name: keep-alive with Go's default MaxIdleConnsPerHost = 2 and 20 workers: few requests wait for a new connection, but hundreds of connections are dialed and thrown away (client TIME_WAIT)
run: tw0=$(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :8080 | wc -l); sw0=$(ip netns exec nl-sockets-server ss -Htan state time-wait sport = :8080 | wc -l); ${BIN}/socklab http -url 'http://198.18.201.10:8080/obj?size=10000' -n 1000 -c 20 ; echo "  new TIME_WAIT — client: $(( $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :8080 | wc -l) - tw0 )), server: $(( $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-server ss -Htan state time-wait sport = :8080 | wc -l) - sw0 ))"

checks.name: MaxIdleConnsPerHost = 20 (≥ concurrency): 20 connections serve all 1000 requests, p50 ≈ 1 RTT, no TIME_WAIT
run: tw0=$(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :8080 | wc -l); sw0=$(ip netns exec nl-sockets-server ss -Htan state time-wait sport = :8080 | wc -l); ${BIN}/socklab http -url 'http://198.18.201.10:8080/obj?size=10000' -n 1000 -c 20 -idle-per-host 20; echo "  new TIME_WAIT — client: $(( $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :8080 | wc -l) - tw0 )), server: $(( $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-server ss -Htan state time-wait sport = :8080 | wc -l) - sw0 ))"

checks.name: the same, but the code never reads the response body: no connection can be reused (1000 dials) — and closing with unread data sends RST, so not even a TIME_WAIT
run: tw0=$(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :8080 | wc -l); sw0=$(ip netns exec nl-sockets-server ss -Htan state time-wait sport = :8080 | wc -l); ${BIN}/socklab http -url 'http://198.18.201.10:8080/obj?size=10000' -n 1000 -c 20 -idle-per-host 20 -drain=false; echo "  new TIME_WAIT — client: $(( $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ss -Htan state time-wait dport = :8080 | wc -l) - tw0 )), server: $(( $(ip netns exec nl-sockets-server ss -Htan state time-wait sport = :8080 | wc -l) - sw0 ))"

checks.name: remove the delay
2000 idle connections to the netpoll server: Go's runtime — a few threads, one epoll instance watching every socket
run: before=$(${BIN}/socklab stat -pid $(cat ${EVIDENCE}/srv-netpoll.pid)); ${BIN}/socklab hold -to 198.18.201.10:7032 -n 2000 -hold 4s > ${EVIDENCE}/hold-netpoll.txt & sleep 3; echo "idle:   $before"; echo "loaded: $(${BIN}/socklab stat -pid $(cat ${EVIDENCE}/srv-netpoll.pid))"; wait; cat ${EVIDENCE}/hold-netpoll.txt

checks.name: 2000 idle connections to the threads server: one OS thread blocked in read() per connection, no epoll registrations
run: before=$(${BIN}/socklab stat -pid $(cat ${EVIDENCE}/srv-threads.pid)); ${BIN}/socklab hold -to 198.18.201.10:7033 -n 2000 -hold 4s > ${EVIDENCE}/hold-threads.txt & sleep 3; echo "idle:   $before"; echo "loaded: $(${BIN}/socklab stat -pid $(cat ${EVIDENCE}/srv-threads.pid))"; wait; cat ${EVIDENCE}/hold-threads.txt

checks.name: a server limited to 64 open files (soft = hard): 100 clients all CONNECT (the kernel completes handshakes into the accept queue), but accept() fails with EMFILE and the rest wait unanswered
run: prlimit --nofile=64:64 ${BIN}/socklab serve -addr 198.18.201.10:7010 -mode greet -id limited -for 8s -pidfile ${EVIDENCE}/lim.pid > ${EVIDENCE}/emfile.log 2>&1 & sleep 0.5; ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ${BIN}/socklab hold -to 198.18.201.10:7010 -n 100 -hold 6s > ${EVIDENCE}/emfile-hold.txt & sleep 1.5; grep 'open files' /proc/$(cat ${EVIDENCE}/lim.pid)/limits; ${BIN}/socklab stat -pid $(cat ${EVIDENCE}/lim.pid); ss -Hltn sport = :7010; ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ${BIN}/socklab greet -to 198.18.201.10:7010 -n 1; wait; cat ${EVIDENCE}/emfile-hold.txt; grep -m2 'accept error' ${EVIDENCE}/emfile.log; echo "accept errors logged: $(grep -c 'accept error' ${EVIDENCE}/emfile.log)"

checks.name: Go raises its own soft limit at start-up (Go 1.19+): started with 64 soft / 8192 hard, it runs with 8191 (hard − 1, by design) — while a shell under the same limits stays at 64
run: prlimit --nofile=64:8192 ${BIN}/socklab serve -addr 198.18.201.10:7011 -for 1s -pidfile ${EVIDENCE}/lim2.pid >/dev/null & sleep 0.3; grep 'open files' /proc/$(cat ${EVIDENCE}/lim2.pid)/limits; prlimit --nofile=64:8192 sh -c 'ulimit -Sn; ulimit -Hn'; wait

checks.name: after a server that closed first exits, its port has TIME_WAITs: bind() without SO_REUSEADDR fails with EADDRINUSE; with it, succeeds
run: ${BIN}/socklab serve -addr 198.18.201.10:7040 -mode close -for 1s >/dev/null & sleep 0.3; ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ${BIN}/socklab hold -to 198.18.201.10:7040 -n 3 -hold 0.5s >/dev/null; wait; ss -Htan sport = :7040; ${BIN}/socklab bind -addr 198.18.201.10:7040; ${BIN}/socklab bind -addr 198.18.201.10:7040 -reuseaddr
expect_contains: (no options): bind() failed: address already in use

checks.name: a port with a live listener: EADDRINUSE even with SO_REUSEADDR, and with SO_REUSEPORT too unless the first listener also set it; ss -ltnp names the owner
run: ${BIN}/socklab serve -addr 198.18.201.10:7041 -mode discard -for 1.5s >/dev/null & sleep 0.3; ${BIN}/socklab bind -addr 198.18.201.10:7041 -reuseaddr; ${BIN}/socklab bind -addr 198.18.201.10:7041 -reuseaddr -reuseport; ss -Hltnp sport = :7041; wait
expect_contains: (SO_REUSEADDR): bind() failed: address already in use

checks.name: three servers on one port with SO_REUSEPORT: the kernel spreads new connections across them by hashing each connection's addresses and ports
run: for i in 1 2 3; do ${BIN}/socklab serve -addr 198.18.201.10:7042 -mode greet -id worker$i -reuseport -for 4s >/dev/null & done; sleep 0.5; ss -Hltn sport = :7042; ip netns exec nl-sockets-client ${BIN}/socklab greet -to 198.18.201.10:7042 -n 300; wait

checks.name: a relay that copies with a fixed buffer, to a backend that never reads: the client's send blocks after ~12 MB (buffers on the way) and the relay stays small
run: echo "before: $(${BIN}/socklab stat -pid $(cat ${EVIDENCE}/relay-copy.pid))"; ${BIN}/tcplab send -to 198.18.201.10:7101 -bytes 200000000 -timeout 5s | grep -E 'transfer|wrote|timed out|never closed'; echo "after:  $(${BIN}/socklab stat -pid $(cat ${EVIDENCE}/relay-copy.pid))"
expect_contains: timed out with data still unsent

checks.name: a relay that queues in memory instead: the client 'delivers' all 200 MB and the relay holds it — RSS grows by the amount the backend did not take
run: echo "before: $(${BIN}/socklab stat -pid $(cat ${EVIDENCE}/relay-unbounded.pid))"; ${BIN}/tcplab send -to 198.18.201.10:7102 -bytes 200000000 -timeout 5s | grep -E 'transfer|wrote|timed out|never closed'; echo "after:  $(${BIN}/socklab stat -pid $(cat ${EVIDENCE}/relay-unbounded.pid))"

checks.name: a UDP consumer that takes 1 ms per datagram, sent 10,000 at once: the default receive buffer (rmem_default) holds a few hundred; the kernel drops the rest and counts UdpRcvbufErrors; the sender is never told
run: sysctl net.core.rmem_default net.core.rmem_max; nstat -n; ${BIN}/socklab udp-sink -addr 198.18.201.10:7200 -per 1ms & sleep 0.3; ${BIN}/socklab udp-blast -to 198.18.201.10:7200 -n 10000; ss -Huanm sport = :7200 | grep -o 'rb[0-9]*,'; wait; nstat -z UdpInDatagrams UdpRcvbufErrors

checks.name: asking for 4 MB with SO_RCVBUF is silently capped at net.core.rmem_max (then doubled); SO_RCVBUFFORCE (root) gets it — more queue, fewer drops, and more delay for what waits in it
run: for a in '-rcvbuf 4194304' '-rcvbuf 4194304 -force'; do nstat -n; ${BIN}/socklab udp-sink -addr 198.18.201.10:7201 -per 1ms $a & sleep 0.3; ${BIN}/socklab udp-blast -to 198.18.201.10:7201 -n 10000 >/dev/null; echo "udp-sink $a: $(ss -Huanm sport = :7201 | grep -o 'rb[0-9]*')"; wait; nstat -z UdpInDatagrams UdpRcvbufErrors | tail -2 | tr '\n' ' '; echo; done
